input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

[RID:web:paper:a39b57e906ed] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2307.10034v2" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.10034v2" title="Validation of Modern JSON Schema: Formalization and Complexity"
JSON Schema is the de-facto standard schema language for JSON data. The language went through many minor revisions, but the most recent versions of the language added two novel features, dynamic references and annotation-dependent validation, that change the evaluation model. Modern JSON Schema is the name used to indicate all versions from Draft 2019-09, which are characterized by these new features, while Classical JSON Schema is used to indicate the previous versions.
  These new "modern" features make the schema language quite difficult to understand, and have generated many discussions about the correct interpretation of their official specifications; for this reason we undertook the task of their formalization. During this process, we also analyzed the complexity of data validation in Modern JSON Schema, with the idea of confirming the PTIME complexity of Classical JSON Schema validation, and we were surprised to discover a completely different truth: data validation, that is expected to be an extremely efficient process, acquires, with Modern JSON Schema features, a PSPACE complexity.

We then prove that its data validation problem is PSPACE-complete. We prove that the origin of the problem lies in dynamic references, and not in annotation-dependent validation. [RID:web:paper:4e549dbb2756] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2503.11288v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.11288v1" title="Elimination of annotation dependencies in validation for Modern JSON Schema"
JSON Schema is a logical language used to define the structure of JSON values. JSON Schema syntax is based on nested schema objects. In all versions of JSON Schema until Draft-07, collectively known as Classical JSON Schema, the semantics of a schema was entirely described by the set of JSON values that it validates. This semantics was the basis for a thorough theoretical study and for the development of tools to decide satisfiability and equivalence of schemas. Unfortunately, Classical JSON Schema suffered a severe limitation in its ability to express extensions of object schemas, which caused the introduction, with Draft 2019-09, of two disruptive features: annotation dependency and dynamic references.
  These new features undermine the previously developed semantic theory, and the algorithms used to decide satisfiability for Classical JSON Schema are not easy to extend. One possible solution is rewriting a schema written in Modern JSON Schema into an equivalent schema in Classical JSON Schema.
  In this paper we prove that the elimination of annotation dependent keywords cannot, in general, avoid an exponential increase of the schema dimension. We provide an algorithm to eliminate these keywords that, despite the theoretical lower bound, behaves quite well in practice, as we verify with an extensive set of experiments.

[RID:web:paper:9bf006e3c429] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2202.12849v3" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.12849v3" title="Witness Generation for JSON Schema"
JSON Schema is an important, evolving standard schema language for families of JSON documents. It is based on a complex combination of structural and Boolean assertions, and features negation and recursion. The static analysis of JSON Schema documents comprises practically relevant problems, including schema satisfiability, inclusion, and equivalence. These three problems can be reduced to witness generation: given a schema, generate an element of the schema, if it exists, and report failure otherwise. Schema satisfiability, inclusion, and equivalence have been shown to be decidable, by reduction to reachability in alternating tree automata. However, no witness generation algorithm has yet been formally described. We contribute a first, direct algorithm for JSON Schema witness generation. We study its effectiveness and efficiency, in experiments over several schema collections, including thousands of real-world schemas. Our focus is on the completeness of the language, where we only exclude the uniqueItems operator, and on the ability of the algorithm to run in a reasonable time on a large set of real-world examples, despite the exponential complexity of the underlying problem.
input.section_draft:
Note on grounding. The text below describes the intended JSON schema and associated validation logic at a conceptual level. Because no retrieved excerpts or run artifacts were provided for this section, the descriptions are presented as general background knowledge and design proposals; they should be instantiated or revised once concrete schema examples, prior outputs, or validator logs are available.

Purpose and design goals (general background knowledge)
- The JSON schema for each generated section is intended to (1) make section contents machine-checkable, (2) require explicit links from factual assertions to evidence, and (3) produce outputs that can be deterministically assembled into LaTeX + refs.bib and audited or edited programmatically.
- The schema is designed to support conservative generation workflows: mandatory evidence fields for factual claims, explicit metadata for provenance, and structured validation results that record any unsupported assertions.

Proposed top-level structure (general background knowledge)
- section_id (string, required): stable identifier for the section node (e.g., ``3.2'' or ``methods-evidence'').
- title (string, required): human-readable section title.
- body (string, required): the section text, preferably in Markdown or LaTeX fragments depending on downstream assembly rules.
- claims (array of claim objects, required): fine-grained, machine-addressable assertions extracted or generated for this section (see claim object below).
- references (array of reference objects, required if any claims cite external material): bibliographic records intended for refs.bib assembly.
- dependencies (array of section_id strings, optional): explicit upstream section nodes that this section depends on for background facts or definitions.
- provenance (object, required): metadata about how this JSON was produced (model identifier, prompt template identifier, generation timestamp).
- validation (object, required): results of automated checks (schema validation status, evidence-coverage summary, unsupported-claim detections, and any validation error messages).
- editor_notes (string, optional): free-text field for human editors indicating required interventions.

Claim object (general background knowledge)
- id (string, required): unique claim identifier within the section.
- text (string, required): the claim phrased as a single declarative sentence or short paragraph.
- claim_type (enum: [``definition'',``measurement'',``method'',``finding'',``background''], optional): coarse label to guide evidence requirements.
- factuality_flag (enum: [``factual'',``speculative'',``opinion''], required): indicates whether the claim must be backed by external evidence; conservative workflows should treat ``factual'' as requiring non-empty evidence_ids.
- evidence_ids (array of evidence identifiers, required if factuality_flag == ``factual''): references to evidence items (these identifiers must map to entries in the references field or to retrieval-result identifiers).
- citation_anchors (array of small strings, optional): textual anchors used in-line to mark where citations should appear in assembled text.
- confidence_score (number, optional): model-reported confidence in the claim; recorded but not used as sole validation logic.
- validation (object, required): per-claim validation outcomes (e.g., evidence_present: bool, unsupported_reason: string|null).

Reference object (general background knowledge)
- ref_id (string, required): stable id used by evidence_ids and for refs.bib assembly.
- bibtex (string, optional but preferred): raw BibTeX entry for assembly.
- title, authors, year, url (fields optional): parsed bibliographic metadata for human review.
- source_id (string, optional): identifier linking back to the retrieval system (e.g., index id or provenance token).

Validation procedure (general background knowledge)
- Syntactic validation: enforce JSON Schema conformance (required fields present and types correct). Failures are reported in validation.schema_errors.
- Evidence-coverage checks: for each claim with factuality_flag == ``factual'', require evidence_ids to be non-empty and map to valid reference objects. Missing evidence yields validation.evidence_coverage_failures.
- Unsupported-claim detection: run an automated heuristic or classifier (record outcome in claim.validation.unsupported_reason) to flag claims that lack adequate support in the injected evidence. The schema records these flags for downstream human review.
- Citation formatting checks: ensure all ref_id values referenced in claims appear in references and that a bibtex or equivalent entry is available for each. Missing bibtex entries are recorded as validation.bib_missing.
- Assembly pre-flight: confirm that required fields for LaTeX assembly (body, references with bibtex, and citation anchors) are present; otherwise, mark as assembly_blockers with explicit messages.

How the schema facilitates edits and audits (general background knowledge)
- Machine-readable claims enable targeted human review: auditors can review only claim objects flagged as unsupported rather than scanning full text.
- Deterministic refs.bib assembly: references are stored as structured records so refs.bib can be emitted programmatically, reducing manual copy errors and improving reproducibility.
- Diff-friendly outputs: JSON outputs can be diffed across generation iterations to isolate changes introduced by model re-runs or prompt edits.
- Traceability: provenance fields link each section to the prompt templates and retrieval artifacts used, supporting reproducible debugging and intervention.

Minimal implementation notes (general background knowledge)
- Use an explicit JSON Schema document to enforce type constraints and required fields at generation time; reject or flag outputs that do not validate.
- Treat claim-level evidence linkage as the primary signal for downstream acceptance: sections with any factual claims lacking evidence should be routed for human intervention before assembly.
- Record all validation failures and keep a validation.log that is shipped with the generated manuscript artifacts for auditing.

Limitations and need for grounded examples
- The above structure is a design proposal and does not include concrete schema files, example generated outputs, or empirical thresholds for automated unsupported-claim detectors. These artifacts are required to finalize the schema and to implement effective validators.
- To proceed from this conceptual schema to an operational one, we request the following retrievals or artifacts (please supply as excerpts or run artifacts):
  - Example JSON outputs from prior generation runs (both passing and failing validation).
  - Any existing JSON Schema files or validator implementations used in related pipeline steps.
  - Logs or annotations from human adjudicators marking unsupported claims (to inform the unsupported-claim detector).
  - Sample refs.bib outputs produced by the assembly step and mapping between ref_id and retrieval-source identifiers.
  - Prompt templates that instruct the generation model to emit the JSON structure (to ensure the schema fields align with model output capabilities).

Concluding remark
- Once concrete examples and validator artifacts are available, the proposed fields and validation logic above can be formalized into a machine-enforceable JSON Schema and integrated into the graph-aware prompting pipeline.

Note on grounding. The text below describes the intended JSON schema and associated validation logic at a conceptual level. Because no concrete schema files, prior-generation JSON outputs, or validator logs were provided for this section, most design decisions and operational rules are presented as general background knowledge and design proposals; these should be instantiated or revised once concrete schema examples, prior outputs, or validator artifacts are available. Where the discussion makes specific factual claims about JSON Schema as a technology, we cite the available literature.

Purpose and design goals (general background knowledge)
- The JSON schema for each generated section is intended to (1) make section contents machine-checkable, (2) require explicit links from factual assertions to evidence, and (3) produce outputs that can be deterministically assembled into LaTeX + refs.bib and audited or edited programmatically. These goals are design choices for conservative, auditable generation workflows (general background knowledge).
- When selecting a schema language, practitioners should be aware that JSON Schema is the de-facto standard for describing the structure of JSON data; recent work documents both the language evolution and practical implications of its modern features \cite{2307.10034v2}. In particular, recent language features (e.g., dynamic references and annotation-dependent validation introduced with Draft 2019-09) materially affect validation semantics and tooling design \cite{2307.10034v2}.

Proposed top-level structure (general background knowledge)
The following top-level keys are proposed for each section JSON document. These fields and their intended semantics are design proposals; concrete type constraints and enum sets should be encoded in a machine-enforceable JSON Schema document before deployment.

- section_id (string, required): stable identifier for the section node (e.g., ``3.2'' or ``methods-evidence'').
- title (string, required): human-readable section title.
- body (string, required): the section text, expressed as Markdown or LaTeX fragments according to downstream assembly rules.
- claims (array of claim objects, required): fine-grained, machine-addressable assertions extracted or generated for this section (see claim object below).
- references (array of reference objects, required if any claims cite external material): bibliographic records intended for refs.bib assembly.
- dependencies (array of section_id strings, optional): explicit upstream section nodes that this section depends on for background facts or definitions.
- provenance (object, required): metadata about how this JSON was produced (model identifier, prompt template identifier, generation timestamp).
- validation (object, required): results of automated checks (schema validation status, evidence-coverage summary, unsupported-claim detections, and any validation error messages).
- editor_notes (string, optional): free-text field for human editors indicating required interventions.

Claim object (general background knowledge)
Each claim is a minimal, machine-addressable unit that links text to evidence and to per-claim validation status. Proposed fields:

- id (string, required): unique claim identifier within the section.
- text (string, required): the claim stated as a single declarative sentence or short paragraph.
- claim_type (enum: [``definition'',``measurement'',``method'',``finding'',``background''], optional): coarse label to guide evidence requirements and reviewer triage.
- factuality_flag (enum: [``factual'',``speculative'',``opinion''], required): indicates whether the claim must be backed by external evidence; conservative workflows should treat ``factual'' as requiring non-empty evidence_ids (general background knowledge).
- evidence_ids (array of evidence identifiers, required if factuality_flag == ``factual''): identifiers that map to entries in the references field or to retrieval-result identifiers.
- citation_anchors (array of short strings, optional): textual anchors used to mark where citations should appear in assembled text.
- confidence_score (number, optional): model-reported confidence in the claim; recorded but not used as sole validation logic (general background knowledge).
- validation (object, required): per-claim validation outcomes (e.g., evidence_present: bool, unsupported_reason: string|null).

Reference object (general background knowledge)
Reference entries provide the information required to assemble refs.bib and to trace evidence back to retrieval artifacts:

- ref_id (string, required): stable id used by evidence_ids and for refs.bib assembly.
- bibtex (string, optional but preferred): raw BibTeX entry for programmatic assembly.
- title, authors, year, url (fields optional): parsed bibliographic metadata for human review.
- source_id (string, optional): identifier linking back to the retrieval system (e.g., index id or provenance token).

Validation procedure
- Syntactic validation: enforce conformance to an explicit JSON Schema document. Practitioners should note that Modern JSON Schema introduces features with complex semantics (dynamic references, annotation-dependent validation); these features have substantial implications for validator implementation and complexity \cite{2307.10034v2}. Formal studies of modern JSON Schema show that some combinations of features increase validation complexity and complicate tooling; implementers should choose schema features with awareness of these trade-offs \cite{2307.10034v2,2503.11288v1}.
- Evidence-coverage checks (general background knowledge): for each claim with factuality_flag == ``factual'', require evidence_ids to be non-empty and to map to valid reference objects. Missing evidence yields entries in validation.evidence_coverage_failures.
- Unsupported-claim detection (general background knowledge): run an automated heuristic or classifier to flag claims that lack adequate support in the injected evidence; record the outcome in claim.validation.unsupported_reason for downstream human review. Prior work on schema analysis and witness generation suggests that tooling for schema-driven generation and checking can be made practical, but completeness and runtime guarantees depend on the selected schema features and the complexity of checks \cite{2202.12849v3,2307.10034v2}.
- Citation formatting and mapping checks (general background knowledge): ensure that all ref_id values referenced in claims appear in references and that a bibtex entry (or equivalent) is available for each; record any missing entries as validation.bib_missing.
- Assembly pre-flight (general background knowledge): confirm that required fields for LaTeX assembly (body, references with bibtex, and citation anchors) are present; otherwise, mark the section with assembly_blockers containing explicit messages.

How the schema facilitates edits and audits (general background knowledge)
- Targeted review: machine-readable claim objects enable auditors to focus review effort on claims flagged as unsupported rather than re-reading entire sections.
- Deterministic refs.bib assembly: storing bibliographic entries as structured records permits programmatic emission of refs.bib, reducing errors from manual transcription.
- Diff-friendly traces: JSON outputs are amenable to textual diffing, enabling reviewers to trace changes across generation iterations and to attribute changes to prompt or retrieval differences.
- Traceability: provenance fields link each section to the prompt templates and retrieval artifacts used, supporting reproducible debugging and intervention.

Minimal implementation notes (general background knowledge)
- Use an explicit JSON Schema document to enforce type constraints and required fields at generation time; reject or flag outputs that do not validate. When choosing which JSON Schema features to use, be mindful that modern constructs (e.g., dynamic references, annotation-dependent validation) affect validator semantics and can increase implementation complexity \cite{2307.10034v2,2503.11288v1}.
- Treat claim-level evidence linkage as the primary signal for downstream acceptance: sections with any factual claims lacking evidence should be routed for human intervention before assembly.
- Record all validation failures and keep a validation.log that is shipped with the generated manuscript artifacts for auditing and reproducibility (general background knowledge).

Limitations and need for grounded examples
- The structure above is a design proposal and does not include concrete schema files, example generated outputs, or validator logs. The theoretical and practical complexities of JSON Schema validation reported in the literature mean that a concrete implementation plan must carefully select schema features and test validators on realistic examples \cite{2307.10034v2,2503.11288v1,2202.12849v3}.
- To operationalize and evaluate this proposal we request the following artifacts (to be supplied as retrievals or run artifacts):
  - Example JSON outputs from prior generation runs (both passing and failing validation).
  - Any existing JSON Schema files or validator implementations used in related pipeline steps.
  - Logs or annotations from human adjudicators marking unsupported claims (to inform unsupported-claim detector calibration).
  - Sample refs.bib outputs produced by the assembly step and the mapping between ref_id and retrieval-source identifiers.
  - Prompt templates that instruct the generation model to emit the JSON structure (to ensure schema fields align with model output capabilities).

Concluding remark (general background knowledge)
- Once concrete examples and validator artifacts are available, the proposed top-level fields, claim/reference structures, and validation logic can be formalized into a machine-enforceable JSON Schema, implemented with a chosen validator, and integrated into the graph-aware prompting pipeline. Practical deployment should explicitly consider known trade-offs in Modern JSON Schema semantics and tooling complexity as documented in the cited literature \cite{2307.10034v2,2503.11288v1,2202.12849v3}.
